clue.text: Poet, American, modelled nude

indicators.note: modelled means shaped or fashioned, so the letters of nude are reworked

explanation.surface: A US poet poses naked as an artist's model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modelled' gives UDEN. W. H. Auden was English-born but took US citizenship in 1946, so 'American' fits the man too.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was an Anglo-American writer of verse, a famous example of a poet.

clue.text: Just recently, beset by inertia; so flat, enervated

indicators.note: the answer is beset, surrounded, by the clue words around it, so it lies concealed inside them

explanation.surface: Someone describes how they have lately felt listless, deflated and drained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beset by' signals the answer sits inside inertiA SO FLAT Enervated.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning lately, in the period leading up to now.

clue.text: Get that sinking feeling as tummy muscles contracted? Flipping pork pie!

indicators.note: contracted means shortened, so the long word for the muscles is cut to its familiar short form

parts.note: the abdominals are the tummy muscles

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the word for the slang is read backwards

parts.note: pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie

explanation.surface: Someone clenching their stomach in dismay at a falsehood, with a mild British exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contracted' cuts ABDOMINALS to ABS, and 'Flipping' turns LIE into EIL. 'Pork pie' is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie.
explanation.definitionFit: To descend a cliff by rope is, playfully, to feel oneself going down steadily.

clue.text: Perrins's partner beginning to fold sheet

parts.note: Lea and Perrins created Worcestershire sauce, so Perrins's partner is Lea

indicators.note: beginning to picks out the first letter of the next word, fold

explanation.surface: Instructions to fold a sheet of paper, perhaps a sauce label.
explanation.walkthrough: Lea & Perrins is the British brand of Worcestershire sauce, named after its two founders.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaf is a single sheet of paper in a book, each with two pages.

clue.text: Sons participating in healthy argument

indicators.note: participating in means taking part inside, so the sons go into the other word

parts.note: hale means healthy, as in hale and hearty
S is the abbreviation for son, so two sons give SS

explanation.surface: Sons joining a lively family dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'participating in' marks the insertion; 'healthy argument' reads as a wholesome debate, hiding the split between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A hassle is a bother or quarrel, a synonym for a dispute between people.

clue.text: Most revealing sketch featuring 1,000 birds (black and white)

indicators.note: a sketch featuring something has it within it, so the other pieces go inside

parts.note: a skit is a short comic sketch
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
pies are magpies, black-and-white birds

explanation.surface: A comedy sketch in which a thousand magpies appear, somehow most revealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'featuring' marks the insertion. 'Pie' is an old word for the magpie, which is why 'pied' means black and white.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimpiest clothes cover the least, so they show off the most of the body.

clue.text: Local visitor's smartest togs, as observed by Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so this calls for that swap

parts.note: best clothes are the smartest ones
togs is British slang for clothes, as is gear

explanation.surface: A pub-goer remarks on a visitor's finest clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: BEST GEAR, with opening sounds swapped, sounds like GUEST BEER. 'Local' is British for the nearby pub, and the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest beer is a brew a pub stocks for a short time, so it is a temporary visitor to the bar.

clue.text: Clumsy Soviet writer speaking

indicators.note: speaking says the writer's name is to be heard, not read

parts.note: Maxim Gorky was a Soviet-era Russian writer

explanation.surface: A Russian author described as an awkward public speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speaking' marks a sound-alike: GORKY, said in a non-rhotic British accent, matches GAWKY.
explanation.definitionFit: Gawky describes someone awkward and ungainly in movement, a synonym for clumsy.

clue.text: Lucky charm mum's put over bed of little 'un

indicators.note: in a down entry, put over means placed above, so the mother comes first

parts.note: mum is ma, so mum's gives MA'S
a cot is a baby's bed

explanation.surface: A mother hangs a good-luck token over her baby's cot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put over' places MAS above COT in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a person, animal or thing believed to bring good fortune, such as a team's emblem.

clue.text: Second shoemaker working the night shift that is shot

parts.note: in the fairy tale The Elves and the Shoemaker, elves make shoes overnight
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A cobbler on nights takes a second photo of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The night-shift shoemaker is one of the Grimms' elves who finish a cobbler's shoes while he sleeps.
explanation.definitionFit: A selfie is a photograph a person takes of themselves, one kind of shot.

clue.text: Following each Morse novel is awe-inspiring

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of Morse take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A fan finds each new Inspector Morse novel wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' gives ROSME. Morse is Colin Dexter's Oxford detective, so the surface reads as a reader's verdict on the books.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fearsome inspires dread or awe by its size or power.

clue.text: Family doctor screening Run Lola Run

indicators.note: screening means shielding or enclosing, so the doctor's letters surround the rest

parts.note: GP, a general practitioner, is the British family doctor

indicators.note: run as in a stocking that runs, coming apart, so the letters of Lola are rearranged

explanation.surface: A family doctor showing the German film Run Lola Run.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Run' is the anagram signal giving ALLO and 'screening' the insertion; the film title disguises both, and only the final 'Run' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallop is a horse's fastest pace, and to gallop is to run fast.

clue.text: With which to contact spin doctor (about time!)

indicators.note: about means around, so the doctor's letters go round the time

parts.note: PR, public relations, is the trade of a spin doctor
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Someone impatiently wants to reach a political spin doctor at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' marks the insertion; '(about time!)' reads as exasperation, but 'time' is a piece and 'about' an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A pager is a small device that receives messages, used to reach doctors on call.

clue.text: A feature of Uncle Richard's canon?

indicators.note: A feature of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about something typical of an uncle's collected works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A feature of' shows the answer inside uncLE RICHard's. 'canon' looks like a body of works, but here it is a churchman.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is a clergyman attached to a cathedral, so one kind of churchman.

clue.text: Pompous matriarch composed odes when touring India

parts.note: a gran, grandmother, heads the family

indicators.note: touring means going around, so the rearranged odes go round the I
composed means put together, so the letters of odes are arranged anew

parts.note: I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A grand old lady writes poems while travelling in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges ODES into DOSE, and 'when touring' wraps it round I to make DIOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandiose describes a showy, overblown manner, so it is a synonym for self-important.

clue.text: Berliner regularly pared cheese

indicators.note: regularly pared means trimmed at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

explanation.surface: A German in Berlin routinely slices cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly pared' keeps the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of Berliner. A Berliner is also a doughnut.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft French cheese with a white rind, an example of the type.

clue.text: Ms Fonteyn shunning Monsieur's vulgar tongue

indicators.note: shunning means avoiding, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: Margot Fonteyn was the great British ballerina

explanation.surface: A ballerina avoids a Frenchman because of his coarse language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shunning' takes M from MARGOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Argot is the slang of a particular group, the kind of street jargon not used in polite speech.

clue.text: Like a desperate male incarcerated

indicators.note: incarcerated means locked up, so the male letter is shut inside the other word

parts.note: a desperate situation is dire

explanation.surface: Something resembling a desperate man in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incarcerated' puts M inside DIRE, after A. 'Like' looks like 'similar to' but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To admire someone is to think well of them, so like is a close synonym as verbs.

clue.text: Special copper put forward point

indicators.note: put forward means moved to the front, so the copper comes ahead of the other letters

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A special constable makes a point at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put forward' moves the metal to the front. 'Special' and 'copper' both suggest British police officers, a deliberate false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: A cusp is a pointed end where two curves meet, such as on a tooth.

clue.text: Animal portion to eat around lunchtime?

indicators.note: to eat around means to take in by surrounding, so the portion's letters enclose the time

parts.note: a chunk is a portion or lump
lunchtime is 1 p.m., written with the 1 as I

explanation.surface: A portion of food to be eaten at about lunchtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to eat around' marks the insertion. Lunchtime is 1pm, written with the numeral one as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A chipmunk is a small striped North American squirrel, an example of an animal.

clue.text: Discover panto theme song

indicators.note: Discover read as dis-cover means strip the covering, so each word loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An instruction to find out what a pantomime's theme tune is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discover' strips the outer letters from each word: pANTo and tHEMe. A panto is a British Christmas stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: An anthem is a rousing song, such as a national hymn or a stadium favourite.

clue.text: Crones pinching Joe Burns's grub

indicators.note: pinching means nabbing or squeezing, so the old women's letters close round the soldier

parts.note: hags are crones, ugly old women
GI Joe is the American soldier, so Joe is a GI

explanation.surface: Old women steal food from a man named Joe Burns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinching' marks the insertion. 'Joe Burns' reads as one name, but Joe is the soldier and Burns is Scotland's national poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns wrote 'Address to a Haggis', so the Scottish pudding is food tied to him.

clue.text: Foreign Secretary half-heartedly nibbled game

indicators.note: half-heartedly means losing half of the heart, one of the two middle letters

parts.note: Dominic Raab was the UK Foreign Secretary
nibbled means bit, took small bites

explanation.surface: A politician only half-heartedly chewed his food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-heartedly' drops one of the two middle letters of RAAB, giving RAB.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbit is an animal hunted for food or sport, so it counts as game.

clue.text: Merry band's leader ignited high explosive

indicators.note: leader picks out the first letter of band's

parts.note: lit means ignited, set alight

explanation.surface: A cheerful bandleader lights a fuse on some high explosive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band's leader' gives B.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe means cheerful and carefree, a synonym for jolly.

clue.text: Dear Meryl; resistance is melting away!

indicators.note: melting away means vanishing, so that letter is removed

parts.note: Meryl Streep is the American actress
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A letter to Meryl Streep saying her opposition is fading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is melting away' takes R from STREEP. 'Dear' looks like a letter's greeting but means pricey.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep price is a high one, so steep and expensive are synonyms.

clue.text: Cautiously trap German lady on vacation

parts.note: a gin is a snare or trap

indicators.note: on vacation means emptied, so only the outside letters of lady stay

explanation.surface: Carefully catching a German woman while she is on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' empties LADY to LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Gingerly means carefully, so as to avoid harm, an adverb of caution.

clue.text: Cart over three feet

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a dray is a heavy cart, as used by brewers

explanation.surface: A cart rolling over someone's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns DRAY backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A yard is the imperial length equal to three feet.

clue.text: Character of pen pal: popular, upfront

indicators.note: upfront means placed at the front, so the popular word comes first

parts.note: in means popular, fashionable
mate is British for a pal

explanation.surface: Describing a well-liked pen pal as frank and open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upfront' sets the order. 'pen pal' looks like a correspondent, but the pen is a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: An inmate is a prisoner, so a person found in the pen, slang for prison.

clue.text: One biting the head of Cleopatra injecting iodine jelly

indicators.note: injecting means putting into, so the iodine goes inside

parts.note: Cleopatra died from the bite of an asp, a snake

indicators.note: the head of picks out the first letter of Cleopatra

parts.note: I is the chemical symbol for iodine

explanation.surface: The snake that bit Cleopatra, injecting venom, retold as iodine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injecting' puts I inside ASP + C.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a savoury jelly made from stock, used to set meat or fish.

clue.text: Angler brewed tea to be guzzled in Russian port

indicators.note: guzzled in means swallowed inside, so the tea goes in the middle
brewed means concocted, so the letters of Angler are mixed up

parts.note: cha is slang for tea

explanation.surface: A fisherman brews tea and gulps it down in a Russian harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brewed' gives ARNGEL and 'to be guzzled in' marks the insertion; 'brewed' and 'guzzled' suit the tea, hiding their jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Archangel (Arkhangelsk) is a seaport on the White Sea in northern Russia.
